lignes.texte: Every tin foil hat theory you’ve heard… might actually be true.
For decades, the military gaslit anyone who said they were conducting false flags,
poisoning soldiers or running psychic spy units.
Turns out, the crazies were right.
For 5 years, one of the most classified weapons over Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh Trail was the rain.
Under Operation Popeye, Air Force crews flew more than 2,600 cloud-seeding sorties over Laos and
Vietnam between 1967 and 1972, pumping silver iodide into monsoon clouds. The goal was to
stretch the rainy season by up to 45 days and turn North Vietnam's supply roads into rivers of mud.
The crews even had an unofficial motto, make mud, not war.
For years, anyone who claimed the US was controlling the weather sounded unhinged. Then
journalist Jack Anderson exposed the program in 1971, and in 1974 a Senate hearing confirmed it.
The fallout was such that the world actually signed a treaty in 1977
specifically banning weather warfare. Which means that, somewhere in international law,
there's a rule that exists because the Air Force tried to weaponize a cloud.
For 2 decades, a slice of America’s intelligence budget went to men sitting
in dark rooms at Fort Meade, Maryland. This wasn’t some secret listening station,
they were trying to see the Soviet Union… with their eyes closed.
Under a rotating cast of codenames, the last and most famous being Stargate,
the Army, the Defense Intelligence Agency, and the CIA spent roughly
$20 million on “remote viewing” experiments from the 1970s until 1995.
Viewers were tasked with locating hostages, Soviet weapons facilities,
and missing aircraft. Basically anything the satellites couldn't catch.
When the CIA had the program independently reviewed in 1995,
the verdict was that it had never produced a single piece of intelligence anyone could act on.
20 years and $20 million later, the CIA’s psychics couldn’t find anything foreign militaries were
hiding. Which is ironic, because their own military was hiding entire bases under the ice.
In 1959, the Army unveiled Camp Century, a warren of scientific research tunnels dug
into the Greenland ice sheet and powered by a portable nuclear reactor. It was a PR dream.
They even flew in an American and a Danish Boy Scout to intern at the base for six months.
What the world didn't see was the real plan behind everything.
Project Iceworm, a scheme to carve thousands of miles of tunnels through the ice and hide
up to 600 nuclear missiles within striking range of the Soviet Union.
The problem? Greenland technically belonged to Denmark, and Denmark officially banned
nuclear weapons on its soil. The truth didn't fully come out until a Danish
government investigation in the 1990s. The ice ended up winning out, too. Glaciers moved,
and the tunnels began crushing themselves within a few years. So the Army left.
It also left behind tons of its diesel fuel, sewage, and radioactive waste,
which scientists now think could resurface as the ice melts.
If you thought leaving nuclear waste for future generations was bad, on the other
side of the Iron Curtain, the Soviets had nuclear waste of their own to dispose of.
The worst nuclear disaster most people have never heard of is named after the wrong town.
On September 29th, 1957, a cooling system failed on an underground tank of radioactive
waste at the Mayak plutonium complex in the Ural Mountains. The tank exploded,
and the blast spread radioactive contamination across thousands of square miles.
Around 10,000 people were evacuated, many never told why. Entire villages
were bulldozed and removed from maps. The disaster is named after the nearby town
of Kyshtym for one reason; Mayak's own city didn't officially exist.
The disaster was rated a level 6 on the international nuclear accident
scale. Only Chernobyl and Fukushima rank higher.
The world only heard about it when exiled Soviet scientist Zhores Medvedev wrote about
it in 1976. Moscow didn't officially admit a thing about it until 1989, 32 years later.
Losing track of radioactive material is one thing. But what about that time
an entire ship full of uranium just…disappeared?
The plot of the 1960s film Dr. Strangelove hinges on the Soviets building an automatic
doomsday machine and neglecting to tell anyone. 2 decades later,
the real Soviet Union built almost exactly that and neglected to tell anyone, either.
The system was called Perimeter, but it's better known by its nickname, Dead Hand.
Operational by 1985, it used sensors to detect nuclear blasts on Soviet
soil. If it registered a blast and lost contact with the military leadership,
officers in a deep bunker could launch special command rockets.
They would fly across the country, broadcasting launch orders to every surviving missile silo.
In other words, killing the Kremlin wouldn't stop the Kremlin's missiles.
Western analysts spent years dismissing rumors of the system before its existence was confirmed
after the Cold War. Russian officials have indicated it's still in service today.
While the Soviets were wiring up the end of the world,
the US Navy was sitting on the bottom of the ocean, listening…
The Sea of Okhotsk was basically the Soviet Union’s private lake during
the Cold War. Which is exactly why, in 1971,
the submarine USS Halibut slipped into it hunting for an undersea communications cable.
They found it the low-tech way, by spotting signs on the shoreline warning ships not to
anchor there. Working 400 feet (122 meters) underwater, Navy divers attached a recording
pod roughly 20 feet (6 meters) long and weighing six tons to the cable,
which picked up conversations without even cutting into it.
Soviet officers assumed nobody could reach that cable, so they barely bothered encrypting
what they said. For years, American subs covertly returned to swap out the tapes.
Operation Ivy Bells ended in 1980, when a broke NSA analyst named Ronald
Pelton walked into the Soviet embassy and sold the whole secret for about $35,000.
Selling out made Pelton a traitor. But the CIA found
its own ways to sell secrets…back to themselves.
Imagine buying the best safe money can buy, then finding out the manufacturer
kept a copy of every key. Now imagine you’re 120 countries doing that exact same thing.
For decades, if a government wanted to keep its secrets safe,
it bought its encryption machines from Crypto AG, a company based in neutral Switzerland.
Nations trusted it with their most sensitive military and diplomatic messages. What they
didn't know was that, since 1970, Crypto AG had been secretly owned by the CIA and West
German intelligence. And they rigged the machines so the messages could be cracked.
Under Operation Rubicon, US spies read Iran's communications during
the hostage crisis and fed Argentina's military messages to Britain during the
Falklands War. And the best part? The targets were paying for the privilege,
which makes this one of the few intelligence operations in history that also turned a profit.
A CIA historian called it "the intelligence coup of the century." It wasn’t until 2020,
that the whole thing was exposed..
Messages are one thing. But the CIA also wanted
to steal a Soviet submarine… while it was 3 miles (4.8 km) underwater.
In 1968, the Soviet submarine K-129 sank in the Pacific with 98 men and nuclear missiles
aboard. The Soviets never found it, but the US did, more than 16,000 feet (4,877 meters) down.
So the CIA built a massive ship with a giant mechanical claw hidden inside
to reach down and grab it. Their cover story was that eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes
was building the Glomar Explorer to mine the ocean floor for minerals.
When Howard Hughes was mentioned, nobody batted an eyelid.
In 1974, Project Azorian actually worked. Well,
partly. The claw broke mid-lift, and only a section of the sub made it up.
Inside were the bodies of 6 Soviet sailors,
whom the CIA buried at sea with full military honors. When reporters started asking questions,
the CIA replied that it could neither confirm nor deny anything.
That phrase is still called the “Glomar response” today. It remains the CIA’s
answer of choice for most questions they’re asked.
Most governments used to respond to Greenpeace protestors with a
strongly-worded statement. France decided to tell off the environmental activists with bombs.
In July 1985, the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior was docked in Auckland,
New Zealand, preparing to sail out and protest French nuclear tests in the
Pacific. Just before midnight, 2 bombs tore through its hull.
Photographer Fernando Pereira went below deck to save his camera equipment and drowned when
the second blast hit. New Zealand police soon arrested 2 suspects posing as a honeymooning
Swiss couple. They were actually agents of France's foreign intelligence service, the DGSE.
France flatly denied it for months, until the Prime Minister admitted French agents had sunk the
ship under orders. The Defense Minister resigned. The agents were sentenced to 10 years in prison,
then transferred to a French Pacific atoll. Both were back home in France within about 2 years.
France at least confessed. The entries staged attacks on themselves and pinned
them on someone else. Welcome to the False Flag Lightning Round!
On the night of September 18th 1931, officers of Japan's Kwantung Army detonated a bomb beside a
Japanese-owned railway near Mukden, in Manchuria. And it was done without approval from their own
government in Tokyo. The Japanese army blamed Chinese soldiers and, within hours, launched
an invasion. Just months later, Japan controlled all of Manchuria and had installed a puppet state.
When a League of Nations investigation concluded the invasion couldn't be
justified as self-defense, Japan's response was simply to quit the League.
Eight years later, Nazi Germany borrowed the same playbook to start the war in Europe.
On the night of August 31st, 1939, SS men in Polish uniforms stormed a German radio station
in the border town of Gleiwitz and broadcast a short anti-German message. Before they left,
they dumped the body of a Polish-sympathizing German man named Franciszek Honiok who
had been drugged and shot by the SS and dressed up to look like a Polish raider.
The next morning, Hitler cited Polish attacks as the rationale
for Germany’s invasion of Poland, and the Second World War officially began.
The man who led the raid, SS officer Alfred Naujocks,
laid out the whole plot in a sworn statement after the war.
And Stalin was taking notes.
On November 26, 1939, the Soviets announced that Finnish artillery
had shelled the border village of Mainila, killing 4 Red Army soldiers.
The USSR demanded an apology. But there was one small problem. The Finnish army
had already pulled its artillery back out of range of the border, specifically to avoid
this kind of incident. Finnish border guards even logged the shots as coming from the Soviet side.
None of that mattered.
Evidence, as it turned out, was optional.
4 days later, the Soviet Union invaded Finland. Historians now broadly agree
the shelling was staged by the Soviets themselves.
The Finns then made the invasion spectacularly unpleasant, but that’s a topic for another time.
How do you turn a country’s clergy against its prime minister? If you’re the CIA in 1953,
you hire people to pretend to be communists and threaten them.
2 years earlier, Iran’s elected Prime Minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country's oil
industry. It was controlled by a British company so London and Washington decided he had to go.
Under Operation Ajax, the CIA and British intelligence set out to topple him, and
one of their tools was a false flag. According to the CIA's own internal history, agents posing as
members of Iran's Communist Tudeh Party threatened Muslim religious leaders. They even staged a fake
bombing of a cleric's home, hoping to scare the clergy into turning against Mossadegh.
And it worked.
In August 1953, Mossadegh was overthrown and the Shah was restored to power. The
CIA didn't officially acknowledge its role in the coup until 2013, 60 years later.
It’s hard to lose 200 tons of, well, anything. But in November 1968,
a freighter called the Scheersberg A left Antwerp with 560 drums of
uranium ore labeled "PLUMBAT," and was supposed to dock in Genoa, Italy.
It never arrived.
Weeks later, the ship turned up in a Turkish port with a different crew, an empty hold,
and pages torn out of its logbook. For years, European nuclear regulators knew
the uranium was gone but said nothing. When the story finally broke in 1977,
the explanation was a heist straight out of a spy novel.
Israeli intelligence had arranged the entire purchase through front companies, and the cargo
was transferred at sea to an Israeli vessel to fuel the country's secret nuclear program.
Time for some Human Guinea Pigs!
Nobody at Porton Down saw nerve gas in the fine print of their terms
and conditions of their stay at the UK’s top secret chemical weapons lab.
For decades, British servicemen were offered extra pay and leave
to take part in tests at Porton Down research facility in rural
England. Many of them believed they were helping find a cure for the common cold.
In May 1953, a 20-year-old RAF engineer named Ronald Maddison sat down for his test.
Scientists dripped a trace amount of pure sarin nerve agent onto a patch of cloth on his arm.
Maddison was dead within hours.
The original inquest was held in secret and attributed the incident to “misadventure.”
It took until 2004, more than 50 years later, and numerous complaints of experiment-related
illnesses at the facility, for a new inquest to rule that Maddison
had been unlawfully killed. The British government eventually paid compensation
to hundreds of Porton Down veterans who were unwillingly subjected to experiments.
In 1955, the Army Chemical Corps bred about a million yellow fever mosquitoes,
loaded them into E14 cluster bombs, and dropped them from 300 feet (91 meters) over Georgia.
Operation Big Buzz sent roughly 330,000 of them out the hatch. They weren't carrying yellow fever,
that would have been the wartime version. But the test was designed to ask 2 important questions.
Can a mosquito survive being bombed? And will it still want dinner afterward?
As it turns out, yes, and very much yes. Traps caught them up to 2,000
feet (610 meters) from the drop zone, feeding on humans and guinea pigs alike.
The sequel, Operation Drop Kick, released even more over Savannah in 1956. Then,
in 1958, the Army let a million loose over Avon Park, Florida.
Between 1962 and 1973, the Pentagon turned its own ships into test tubes as part of
Project 112 and its naval branch, SHAD, or Shipboard Hazard Defense.
Planes and boats sprayed Navy vessels with nerve agents like VX and sarin,
and bacteria like E. coli to see how an attack would spread through a ship.
The tests read like a Pentagon cologne line. Autumn Gold. Copper Head. Folded Arrow.
Many of the nearly 5,800 service members involved had no idea they were in one.
The files stayed classified until 2000. And while the Pentagon spent decades hiding SHAD,
in 1991, it found something new to deny.
On March 4th, 1991, days after the Gulf War ended, U.S. combat engineers blew up an Iraqi
ammunition bunker. Six 6 later, they blew up a pit of rockets next door for good measure.
Inside were 122-millimeter rockets loaded with sarin and cyclosarin nerve agents.
In October of the same year, UN inspectors found evidence of chemical weapons,
but it wasn’t until 1993 that the Pentagon officially concluded that
no troops had been exposed. It took until June 1996 to admit what happened.
Its estimate of troops who may have been under the plume came to 98,900.
By 2000, that number was over 100,000.
Government auditors later ruled that the Pentagon's exposure conclusions could not
be adequately supported. But if the Pentagon exposed its troops overseas by accident,
in St. Louis, the Army sprayed American families on purpose…
The 1950s and 1960s were a wild time for military conspiracies,
especially if you were a resident of St. Louis.
If you were, you were told that the Army would be testing a smokescreen to hide the city from
Soviet radar. Nobody thought to explain why hiding a city from radar required spraying
its playgrounds. What actually came out of the blowers on rooftops and in the backs of
station wagons was zinc cadmium sulfide, sprayed to simulate how a biological attack would spread.
The Army's own records described one target area as a “densely populated slum district.”
It was about 75% Black, and it included the Pruitt-Igoe housing project. The Army says
follow-up studies found no health risk. But survivors point to a government study
warning that repeated exposure could cause kidney and bone damage and lung cancer,
and they're still fighting for compensation.
If you thought that was bad, wait until you hear what Apartheid South Africa did.
In the 1980s, apartheid South Africa’s military built a secret chemical and
biological weapons program called Project Coast. It was hidden behind front companies
with names like Delta G Scientific and Roodeplaat Research Laboratories.
While the labs worked on anthrax, cholera, and nerve agents, almost a fifth of the projects
were about fertility. The research involved fertility-control vaccines,
adding an even more horrific dimension to this program. Those contraceptives
would be given solely to black people to make them sterile without their knowing.
As the program was uncovered, its leader, army cardiologist Wouter Basson, was accused of
supplying poison slipped into tea, soft drinks, and beer to kill anti-apartheid activists. The
program also mass-produced ecstasy, which is how Basson ended up in handcuffs. In 1997,
narcotics agents caught him trying to sell 100,000 tablets. As they closed in,
he dived into a dam in a futile attempt to escape. It didn’t work.
He was tried on 67 charges, 16 of them murder. The judge threw out the counts covering some 200
deaths in Namibia, ruling that South African courts couldn't try crimes committed abroad.
He called the rest of the prosecution's case too fragmented and confusing. So,
in 2002, Dr. Death walked out of court acquitted.
South Africa’s poison labs were kept secret on purpose. In the
Soviet Union, the secret got out, literally, through an air filter.
In April 1979, people in the Soviet city of Sverdlovsk started dying of anthrax.
At least 64 were killed. Moscow blamed tainted black market meat,
and the KGB confiscated hospital records to keep that story straight.
The real source was Compound 19, a military plant that made dried
anthrax spores for weapons. According to a top Soviet bioweapons scientist who later defected,
workers had simply forgotten to replace a filter on an exhaust system.
In the long history of skipped maintenance, this one is hard to top.
13 years later in 1992, Harvard's Matthew Meselson and his team mapped where each victim
had been that day. The victims fell along a straight line, directly downwind of the
plant. That same year, Russian President Boris Yeltsin admitted the military was responsible.
He would know. In 1979, he'd been Sverdlovsk's Communist Party boss.
Meanwhile, NATO was busy hiding entire armies in Western Europe…
After World War II, Western intelligence agencies were worried that if the Soviets rolled into
Western Europe, there'd be no one left to fight back. So, working with NATO, they built secret
“stay-behind” networks in countries across the continent. They were composed of trained
civilians and operatives with buried stashes of weapons and explosives.
Think of it as a resistance movement,
pre-assembled, with all the explosives and guns included.
The public found out in 1990, when Italy’s Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti admitted to
parliament that Italy's branch, called Gladio, had existed for decades. The revelation caused chaos,
especially in Italy where investigators had already been examining links between far-right
extremists and deadly bombings during the country's “Years of Lead.” The European
Parliament passed a resolution condemning the networks and demanding full investigations.
Fortunately, NATO's secret armies never had to fire a shot at the Soviets. In Northern Ireland,
very public British soldiers fired on citizens, and then the government covered for them.
On January 30th, 1972, British paratroopers opened fire on a civil rights march in Derry,
Northern Ireland. Twenty-six unarmed civilians were shot. 14 of them died.
An official inquiry led by Lord Widgery largely cleared the soldiers just 11
weeks later. He also suggested some of the victims had been handling guns or nail bombs.
In 1998, the government opened a new inquiry. It took 12 years and cost nearly £200 million
to finalize, roughly £5 million for every year of denial. But in 2010, the Saville Report concluded
that none of the victims had posed any threat and that the killings were unjustified and
unjustifiable. Then Prime Minister David Cameron stood up in Parliament and apologized, and in
2025, the only soldier ever brought to trial over the Bloody Sunday killings was acquitted.
Britain spent almost four decades protecting its own soldiers, after World War II,
but the U.S. protected someone else’s…. including some of the worst war criminals of the century.
In occupied China, Japan’s Unit 731 famously ran some of the worst experimental programs of the
20th century. Under General Shiro Ishii, doctors infected prisoners with plague,
cholera, and anthrax, performed vivisections on living people,
and dropped plague-infected fleas over Chinese cities.
Thousands died inside the facility itself, and far more died in the field attacks. After the war,
American officials made a deal: immunity in exchange for their research on biological weapons.
None of the unit's leaders faced a war crimes trial in Tokyo, and several went
on to comfortable careers in Japanese medicine and business. When the Soviets put a handful
of Unit 731 members on trial in 1949, the US dismissed it as communist propaganda.
Hiding someone else's war crimes is bad. But the Soviets managed to blame
their own massacre on the Nazis, and nearly got away with it at Nuremberg…
In the spring of 1940, the Soviet secret police rounded up about 22,000 Polish army officers,
police, doctors, lawyers, and teachers and shot them. Most were killed with a
single bullet to the back of the head. The order had been signed by Stalin himself.
When German troops discovered the mass graves in Katyn Forest in 1943, Moscow blamed the Nazis.
The Soviets even tried to add Katyn to the list of German crimes at the Nuremberg trials.
Meanwhile, the US and British governments, not wanting to anger a wartime ally,
buried their own evidence pointing at Moscow. The lie survived until April 1990,
when the Soviet Union admitted the NKVD was responsible.
And in 2010, the story added one last cruel twist. Poland's president and dozens of the country's top
officials died in a plane crash on their way to the 70th anniversary memorial at Katyn.
In October 1990, two months after Iraq invaded Kuwait,
a tearful 15-year-old girl identified only as Nayirah testified before a US
congressional caucus. She said she'd watched Iraqi soldiers pull premature babies out
of hospital incubators in Kuwait before “leaving them to die on the cold floor.”
President George H.W. Bush repeated it again and again. Several senators cited it in the debate
before the vote to authorize war, a vote that passed the Senate by just five votes.
In 1992, it came out that Nayirah was the daughter of Kuwait's ambassador to the
United States. Her testimony had been arranged by the PR giant Hill & Knowlton, which was paid
millions by a Kuwaiti government-backed group called Citizens for a Free Kuwait.
Later investigations found no credible evidence the incubator story ever happened.
Congress had been moved to tears by a client pitch.
Faking a story to start a war is bad. Faking one about your own dead hero,
then lying to his family, somehow feels even worse…
Pat Tillman turned down a multimillion-dollar NFL contract with the Arizona Cardinals to become
an Army Ranger after 9/11. The Army repaid him by turning his death into a recruiting poster.
It was extremely patriotic, and much publicized.
On April 22nd, 2004, Tillman had paid the ultimate sacrifice and was killed in Afghanistan.
The Army told the public and his family he died charging up a hill at enemy fighters,
and awarded him a Silver Star for heroism. In reality,
Tillman had been killed by his fellow Rangers in a friendly-fire accident…
And the Army knew it almost immediately.
Soldiers burned his uniform and body armor. A general sent a memo warning top
officials that it was highly possible Tillman had died from friendly fire,
so that the President wouldn't unknowingly repeat the heroic version in a speech.
Nobody thought to send that memo to his family. Meanwhile, they sat through a nationally
televised memorial built on the fake story. They weren't told the truth for more than a month.
Pentagon investigators later faulted several senior officers,
including 4 generals, for how it was handled.
On November 15, 1977, a 13-year-old Japanese girl named Megumi Yokota
walked home from badminton practice in the coastal city of Niigata. She never arrived.
For years, Japanese people kept vanishing from beaches along the country's western coast. Some
people pointed the finger squarely at North Korea, but were written off as conspiracy theorists.
Then, in 2002, North Korean leader Kim Jong-il sat down with Japan's Prime Minister and
admitted that North Korean agents had abducted 13 Japanese citizens several decades before.
Some were used to teach spies how to speak and act Japanese. 5 were
allowed to return home. North Korea claimed the rest, including Megumi,
were dead. When Pyongyang later handed over remains it said were hers, Japanese DNA
testing concluded they belonged to someone else. Japan officially recognizes 17 abductees today.
Our number one entry is the conspiracy theory that ate itself…
In 1983, a small pro-Soviet newspaper in India printed an anonymous letter from
an allegedly well-known American scientist. It claimed that AIDS,
a terrifying new disease at the time, had been created by the Pentagon as a biological weapon.
In 1985, a Soviet newspaper repeated the claim and cited the Indian article
as its source. East Germany's secret police, the Stasi, then helped push a
pseudo-scientific report blaming the Army's biological research lab at Fort Detrick,
Maryland. Within a few years, the story had run in the media in more than 80 countries.
The whole thing was a part of Operation INFEKTION, a KGB disinformation campaign
built to turn the world against the US military. In 1992, the head of
Russia's foreign intelligence service, Yevgeny Primakov, admitted the KGB had been behind it.
The story had a life of its own, and it's still repeated today. So
the craziest military conspiracy on this list is one that never happened,
invented by a very real conspiracy that did.
